client: I've been really struggling at work since my grandma passed away last month. Every time I try to focus, I just start remembering all these little moments with her and it completely derails me. I'm not sure talking about it will help - the pain feels too fresh and I don't see how anything can change the fact that she's gone.
therapist:
I hear how deeply you're grieving your grandmother, and how these precious memories are making it hard to focus at work right now. It's completely understandable to feel this raw pain so soon after your loss—would you be willing to explore how these memories might coexist with your work, rather than derail it?  

The sadness you're describing sounds like it's sitting with you constantly—have you noticed any moments, even brief ones, when the weight feels slightly lighter?

client:
I don't know if I want those memories to coexist with work—it feels disrespectful somehow, like I should be fully present in my grief. And no, the weight never lifts, not even for a second. When I try to focus on spreadsheets, all I see is her hands knitting in her favorite chair.  

I know you're trying to help, but this just feels... impossible right now. How can anything feel lighter when she's gone forever?
therapist:
It sounds like you're holding onto this grief so tightly because it feels like the only way to honor her—like letting go even a little might mean losing her all over again. That devotion to your grandmother's memory is so deeply loving, even though it's leaving you exhausted.  

I wonder if we could gently explore what "disrespectful" means in this context—do you think she would want you to carry this pain without relief?

client:
I know logically she wouldn't want me to suffer like this, but it still feels wrong to feel better. Like if I'm not constantly grieving, I'm forgetting her or something. The pain is the only thing that still connects me to her. 

I get what you're saying about it being loving, but it doesn't feel loving—it just feels like failure. Like I'm failing at grieving properly.
therapist:
You're describing such a painful bind—where the grief feels like both a connection and a burden, and any relief comes with guilt. That tension between knowing what she'd want for you and feeling like you're betraying her by considering it must be so heavy to hold.  

Could we try something different? Instead of focusing on letting go of the pain, what if we explored how to honor her in ways that might also bring you moments of comfort? What's one small thing she loved that could become a gentle ritual for you?

client: I like the idea of honoring her, but I'm not sure if I can do it without feeling worse. She loved gardening, but every time I see her roses in the yard, I just feel this crushing sadness. Maybe it's too soon for something like that?
therapist:
It makes sense that even positive connections to her—like the roses—feel overwhelming right now. Grief has its own timeline, and it's okay if certain things still feel too tender to approach.  

What if we started even smaller than the garden? Maybe just noticing one rosebud from the window, or remembering how she'd hum while pruning—not pushing through the sadness, but letting it be there alongside the love? Would that feel more manageable?

client: I don't know... even looking at roses from the window makes my chest feel tight. It's like the second I notice them, all the memories come rushing back at once. Maybe it's stupid, but part of me feels guilty when I try to remember the happy moments—like I don't deserve to feel comfort from them after everything.
therapist:
The guilt you're describing sounds like it's wrapping around all these memories, making even the beautiful ones feel painful right now. It's not stupid at all—it shows just how much you loved her, and how complicated grief can be.  

Instead of pushing toward the roses yet, would it feel safer to start with something more neutral—maybe another small way she showed her love that doesn't feel as charged? Like a recipe she made, or a phrase she used to say?

client:
I guess she did always make this really simple pasta dish when I was sick. But even that makes me feel guilty now—like I took her for granted when she was doing all these little things for me. It's like every memory just reminds me of how much I didn't appreciate her enough. 

I don't know if focusing on neutral things will help. The guilt just follows me everywhere, even into the small memories.
therapist:
It sounds like the guilt is weaving itself into every memory, even the ones that were meant to bring comfort. That must be so exhausting—to feel like you can't hold onto anything without it turning into regret.  

I wonder if we could gently challenge that thought about not appreciating her enough—what would she say if she heard you say that? Do you think she saw your love in ways you might not be seeing right now?

client: I don’t know what she’d say—I think she’d try to reassure me, but it feels like that doesn’t count because she was always so kind and forgiving. I keep replaying moments where I was distracted or stressed instead of fully present with her, and it’s like those are the only memories that stick now. It’s hard to imagine she saw my love when I feel like I failed her so often.
therapist:
It's heartbreaking to hear how these moments of perceived failure are overshadowing all the ways you showed your love—your grandmother's kindness seems to have become another reason to doubt yourself, rather than a gift she freely gave. That pattern of focusing only on what you think you did wrong must make the grief feel even heavier.  

When you think about those times you were distracted or stressed, is there any chance she might have understood those moments differently than you're remembering them now? What might she have known about your life that you're not factoring in?

client:
I’ve never thought about it that way before. My grandma always seemed so patient and understanding, but I keep focusing on the times I wasn’t there or wasn’t fully present. It’s hard to imagine she wouldn’t have been disappointed in me, though. I feel like I let her down, and now I can’t fix it.  

I guess she did know how busy and stressed I was with work and everything else. But I still feel like I should have done more, like I should have been better. It’s hard to let go of that guilt, even if she might have understood.
therapist:
It sounds like you're holding yourself to an impossibly high standard—one that even your grandmother, with all her understanding, wouldn't have expected of you. Grief has a way of sharpening our self-criticism, making "should haves" feel much louder than the reality of how love actually works between people.  

What would it feel like to experiment with holding two truths at once: that you wish you'd done some things differently, *and* that your love for her was still clear in countless other ways? Could we try naming one small way she might have felt your care, even during your busiest times?

client:
I get what you're saying about holding two truths, but it's hard to focus on the good when the regrets feel so heavy. Like, I know I called her every Sunday, but I keep thinking about how I canceled our last lunch date because work was crazy. 

The idea that she felt my care... maybe when I sent her those funny cat videos? She always texted back laughing emojis. But then I think - was that enough? Shouldn't I have been there more in person?
therapist:
It sounds like you're wrestling with whether those smaller acts of love—like the cat videos—were "enough," even though they clearly brought her joy. That tension between what you did and what you wish you'd done must feel so heavy right now.  

I wonder if we could gently explore what "enough" means in this context—do you think your grandmother measured your love by the number of lunches you shared, or by the consistent ways you showed up for her, even from a distance?

client:
I know logically that she wouldn't have kept sending me those silly cat videos if she didn't feel loved, but I can't shake this nagging guilt that I should've done more. Even little things—like not calling her back fast enough sometimes—feel like huge failures now that she's gone. 

The idea of "enough" just makes me feel worse, because it feels like there's some imaginary standard I didn't meet. How do you measure something like love anyway? It's not like I can ask her now.
therapist:
You're touching on something so profound here—how grief can turn love into a math problem we feel we failed, when in reality, love was never about perfect scores. It sounds like you're caught between knowing her love was unconditional and still feeling like you didn't earn it fully.  

What if we tried shifting from measuring "enough" to noticing the *quality* of those connections? When she sent those laughing emojis, what do you think she was actually telling you about how she felt in those moments?
